text: To be written out of history
He was to become the most quoted economist of his generation.
She would go on to found three institutions, none of which survived her.
He was about to abandon it altogether when the letter arrived.
Neither of them was ever to see the result.
The hardest part of a biography is not the research. It is deciding, on page one, what the life was for — and then trying not to let that decision write the rest of the book.
But you already know how it ends. Every sentence you write is written by somebody who knows.
Which is why the language gives itself away. The moment I write she was to spend eleven years in Bologna, I have told the reader that those years mattered, before I have shown them anything.
And the decade she was overshadowed — the one she never mentioned. How do you write ten years of silence?
Badly, in the first draft. I had her waiting for the letter from Bologna, which made the decade a prologue. It was not a prologue to her. It was ten years.
That is the honest problem with the form. Nothing in a life is a prologue while you are living it.
No. And the paper she wrote in a fortnight, the one that was to be vindicated thirty years later — she filed it under distractions. I have the folder.
Which is either very consoling or extremely alarming, and I have not decided which.
He was about to abandon it when the letter arrived.
The paper she filed under distractions was to be vindicated thirty years later.

People assume the difficult part is the research. It is not. The difficult part is the first sentence, because the first sentence has to decide what the life was about, and it has to do it in one line, before anybody has read anything else. Get that wrong and the other nine hundred words are an argument with your own opening. The best ones to write, by a long way, are the people nobody has heard of. A woman who ran the same shop for fifty-one years. A man who kept the records of a football club that no longer exists. You have no template, so you have to find out what the life actually was. And there is one sentence I have never written and never will. I do not write that somebody lost a battle with an illness. Nobody loses a battle by dying. It was never a battle and they never agreed to fight it.

I want to make an objection to the whole form, and I should say at the start that I read biographies constantly and enjoy them enormously, so take this as a family argument. My objection is this. A biography imposes a shape that nobody had while they were living. Look at the grammar and you can watch it happening. He was to become. She was never to see. Those forms are only available to somebody standing at the end of the story, and every time one appears, a decision has been taken about what mattered, on evidence the subject never had. The years that look like a prologue were not a prologue to the person living them. They were eleven years, and they were the whole of their thirties, and at no point did anybody feel that they were waiting for the letter from Bologna.

Marta says the hardest part is deciding on page one what the life was for. He points out that every sentence is written by somebody who already knows the ending. She agrees, and shows how the grammar gives the writer away. He asks how she wrote the decade the subject never mentioned. She admits that her first draft turned ten real years into a prologue.
